provenance: American Associated Artist's, New York | | Lot Essay | | Between 1937 and 1941, Grant Wood created 19 lithographs that were published by Associated American Artists (A.A.A.) but his 1937 print, Sultry Night, is the rarest and most unique. The A.A.A, was a Depression-era enterprise that sold original prints by American artists, offering printed images of American life in large editions, at reasonable prices, via mail order and through regional stores. Following the unveiling of the oil version of Sultry Night in early 1937 — an image inspired by Wood's childhood memories of farmhands — the lithograph was created and made available through the A.A.A. catalogue. This lithograph gained notoriety for its full-frontal portrayal of a nude man and the U.S. Post Office banned A.A.A. from mailing the print because it was considered obscene. As a result, only 100 impressions were made.

title: Das Graphische Werk von Egon Schiele
description: Das Graphische Werk von Egon Schiele (Kallir 3-8, 16-17), 1914-18/1922 The complete set of eight prints, including six etchings and two lithographs on wove paper, numbered in ink '42' on the justification page, from the edition of 80 (Kallir states some bear the artist's stamped signature verso), published by Rikola Verlag, Verlag Neuer Graphik, Vienna-Berlin-Leipzig-Munich, with title, introduction text in German by Arthur Roessler and justification page, loose (as issued), contained in original green paper-covered portfolio. Titles Include: Portrait of a Man; Self-Portrait; Portrait of Franz Hauer; Squatting Woman; Sorrow; Portrait of Arthur Roessler; Portrait of Paris von Gütersloh; Girl various sizes portfolio 28 1/2 x 21in (72.4 x 53.3cm)
provenance: Felix Landau Gallery, Los Angeles | Acquired directly from above by the present owner | | Lot Essay | | Egon Schiele's print portfolio is a rare and compelling extension of his singular artistic vision. Known for his psychologically intense portraits and provocative nudes, Schiele translated these themes into the medium of printmaking with remarkable precision and raw energy. Though he only created seventeen prints during his short career, these works encapsulate his distinctive style — angular, expressive, and unflinchingly direct. | | Among the key works in this collection is Kauernde (Squatting Woman), in which Schiele manipulates his signature sinuous lines to capture both the vulnerability and defiance of the female form. The contorted posture and stark contrast between flesh and background enhance the sense of unease that pervades much of his work. Similarly, Kümmernis (Sorrow) echoes motifs found in his paintings of mothers, evoking themes of creation, suffering, and artistic transformation. | | Schiele's portraits of his patrons, Arthur Roessler and Franz Hauer, are equally revelatory. These figures were integral to his career, supporting him financially and encouraging his artistic experiments. The intensity of their expressions, heightened by Schiele's jagged contours and stripped-down compositions, underscores his ability to pierce the psychological depth of his subjects. | | The portfolio also includes two lithographs commissioned in 1918 but ultimately rejected — one being Mädchen (Girl), deemed too explicit due to its depiction of adolescent sexuality. This rejection speaks to Schiele's persistent challenge to social norms and his exploration of human vulnerability, desire, and mortality. | | Despite Roessler's efforts to introduce Schiele to printmaking as a means of financial security, these works were never published during the artist's lifetime. It was only after his untimely death from influenza in 1918 that Otto Nirenstein facilitated their publication. In 1922, Das Graphische Werk von Egon Schiele (The Graphic Work of Egon Schiele) was released, preserving Schiele's entire body of printed work — his last two lithographs and six drypoints — offering a rare glimpse into the latest chapter of the artist's career. | | Ultimately, Schiele's prints stand as a testament to his unwavering artistic vision. Even in this relatively limited output, his ability to render human figures with an unsettling honesty and emotional depth remains unparalleled. The portfolio not only extends his legacy beyond painting but also underscores the urgency and intensity that defined his brief yet extraordinary career.

Birtwell, a renowned textile designer, became a key figure in Hockney's world in the 1960s, and he captured her likeness in numerous drawings, paintings, and prints. He was drawn to her playful and humorous nature, once remarking, "When I first met her, I was attracted to the fact that she could make me laugh." His portraits of Celia are characterized by a tenderness and intimacy that reflect their close relationship, often emphasizing her distinctive features — her wavy hair, expressive eyes, and graceful presence. | | Hockney's depictions of Celia not only showcase his mastery of line and color but also serve as a visual record of their lifelong connection, enduring personal changes, and the evolving art world. provenance: David Bowie, New York | Pat Gibbons, New York (a gift from the above before 1980) | Sotheby's New York, 15 Nov 2016, Lot 349 | Private Collection, Los Angeles | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Lot Essay | | Objet indestructible combines Man Ray's most iconic practices: the readymade and photography. Tucked into a sleek wooden box, the work consists of a metronome with a striking image of Lee Miller's eye attached to the central pendulum. Man Ray first attached a photograph of an eye to a metronome in 1923 while working in his studio, using the pendulum's rhythm to regulate his brushstrokes. He titled the creation Objet à détruire (Object to destroy). One day as the metronome came to a halt, he did exactly that and smashed the object with a hammer in a moment of fury. | | In 1933 he recreated the original, using the eye of Lee Miller, famed photographer and model, as well as Man Ray's recent ex-lover and muse. He published a drawing of the object in This Quarter and included the following instructions: 'Cut out the eye from a photograph of one who has been loved but is seen no more. Attach the eye to the pendulum of a metronome and regulate the weight to suit the tempo desired [then with] a hammer well-aimed, try to destroy the whole at a single blow.' | | In 1965, Man Ray collaborated with Daniel Spoerri's publishing house, Édition MAT, to produce an edition of 100. This edition was renamed Objet indestructible (Indestructible Object), an ode to Man Ray's reconciliation with Lee Miller as lifelong friends. The present example was previously in the esteemed collection of legendary rock star, David Bowie, and was later gifted to his tour manager, Pat Gibbons.
